title: Fake news, information overload, and the third-person effect in China
screen_reason: National online survey of 1,111 Chinese adults (2-6 August 2018). Although the paper's aim is the third-person effect, the Findings section reports several descriptive shares with the full-sample denominator: 46.2% frequently came across fake news in the past 6 months; 5.7% 'often' and 30.9% 'sometimes' shared a news story later found to be fake; and perceived-amount shares for online news media (37.2% at least 'some' made up, 10% 'most') and social media (44% at least 'some', 12% 'most'). Self-reported encounter and sharing shares plus perceived amount of misinformation in the environment are all in scope, so INCLUDE.

estimates.platform: Survey (all media; no channel specified for this item)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report frequently coming across fake news stories in the past 6 months
estimates.value_raw: Nearly half (46.2%) of the respondents reported frequently coming across fake news stories in the past 6 months
estimates.denominator: 1,111 Chinese adults on a national research-only online panel (Impression Boguan Network Technology / Sina Data Solution), cooperation rate 40.5%
estimates.definition: Respondent's answer to 'how often they came across news stories that they thought were fake in the past 6 months' (1 = never; 4 = often); the paper reports the share answering 'frequently'
estimates.misinfo_def: In this study, we define “fake news” as “news stories that are completely made up.”
estimates.source_quote: Nearly half (46.2%) of the respondents reported frequently coming across fake news stories in the past 6 months.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report on a 4-point frequency scale (1 = never, 4 = often); respondents judged for themselves what counted as fake, cued by the definition 'news stories that are completely made up'. The authors list the narrow definition as a limitation.
estimates.moderator_quote: The study is based on a national online survey conducted from August 2 to 6, 2018 with a national sample of 1111 Chinese adults from China’s 22 provinces, five autonomous regions, and four municipalities. ... The cooperation rate was 40.5%.
estimates.notes: Ambiguity flagged: the item is a 4-point scale (never / ... / often) but the paper reports a single figure for 'frequently' without saying whether it is the top category alone or the top two collapsed; the underlying distribution is not printed. Non-probability opt-in online panel; the authors note the sample skews more female, younger, better educated and higher income than the CNNIC benchmark of Chinese internet users, and that the frame is internet users, not the whole Chinese population. The preceding sentence ('The survey results suggest that fake news has become a significant concern among Chinese citizens.') is mangled by the PDF text extraction, so only the value sentence is quoted.

estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they OFTEN shared a news story on social media that they later found to be fake
estimates.value_raw: had “often” (5.7%) or “sometimes” (30.9%) shared news stories on social media that they later found to be fake
estimates.denominator: 1,111 Chinese adults on a national research-only online panel, cooperation rate 40.5%
estimates.definition: Respondent chose 'often' when asked how often they had shared a news story on social media that they later found to be fake (1 = never; 4 = often)
estimates.misinfo_def: In this study, we define “fake news” as “news stories that are completely made up.”
estimates.source_quote: More than one-third also said that they had “often” (5.7%) or “sometimes” (30.9%) shared news stories on social media that they later found to be fake.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report; requires the respondent to have later discovered the story was fake, so it is bounded below by awareness
estimates.moderator_quote: respondents were asked how often they came across news stories that they thought were fake in the past 6 months and how often they had shared a news story on social media that later they found to be fake (1 = never; 4 = often)
estimates.notes: Strict ('often') response option only. The paper's own summary 'more than one-third' is the sum 5.7 + 30.9 = 36.6%, which R8 forbids computing, so the two options are recorded separately (see the companion 'sometimes' row). No time window is attached to the sharing item.

estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they SOMETIMES shared a news story on social media that they later found to be fake
estimates.value_raw: had “often” (5.7%) or “sometimes” (30.9%) shared news stories on social media that they later found to be fake
estimates.denominator: 1,111 Chinese adults on a national research-only online panel, cooperation rate 40.5%
estimates.definition: Respondent chose 'sometimes' when asked how often they had shared a news story on social media that they later found to be fake (1 = never; 4 = often)
estimates.misinfo_def: In this study, we define “fake news” as “news stories that are completely made up.”
estimates.source_quote: More than one-third also said that they had “often” (5.7%) or “sometimes” (30.9%) shared news stories on social media that they later found to be fake.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report; requires the respondent to have later discovered the story was fake
estimates.moderator_quote: how often they had shared a news story on social media that later they found to be fake (1 = never; 4 = often)
estimates.notes: Middle response option of the same item as the 5.7% 'often' row; marked definition_variant. An analyst wanting 'shared any' would need 5.7 + 30.9 = 36.6% ('more than one-third' in the paper's words), which R8 does not permit as an extracted value.

estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who think at least 'some' of the online news stories they encountered in the past 6 months were completely made up
estimates.value_raw: more than one-third (37.2%) of the respondents said that at least “some” of the news stories they encountered in the past 6 months were completely made up and another 10% said “most” of them were fake
estimates.denominator: 1,111 Chinese adults on a national research-only online panel, cooperation rate 40.5%
estimates.definition: Respondent's answer to how many of the news stories in online media they believed to be entirely made up (1 = none of them; 5 = all of them); numerator = those answering at least 'some'
estimates.misinfo_def: In this study, we define “fake news” as “news stories that are completely made up.”
estimates.source_quote: When asked about how many of the news stories in online news media they thought were fake, more than one-third (37.2%) of the respondents said that at least “some” of the news stories they encountered in the past 6 months were completely made up and another 10% said “most” of them were fake.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Perceived amount of fake news in the respondent's own online news environment, self-reported on a 5-point 'none of them ... all of them' scale
estimates.moderator_quote: They were also asked how many of the news stories on social media or on online media they believed to be entirely made up (1 = none of them; 5 = all of them).
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE on two counts. (a) This is a perceived-AMOUNT item (how much of what I see is fake), which the protocol admits, rather than an encounter share. (b) The sentence is internally ambiguous: '37.2% said at least some ... and another 10% said most' reads as though 37.2% is the 'some' category and 10% a further 'most' category, in which case a true 'at least some' figure would be higher; taken literally, 'at least some' already includes 'most'. Recorded as printed. The stricter 'most' figure (10%) is not extracted as a separate row.

estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who believe at least 'some' of the news stories on social media are fake
estimates.value_raw: nearly half (44%) of the respondents believed that at least “some” of the stories on social media were fake, and 12% thought that “most” of the news on social media was made up
estimates.denominator: 1,111 Chinese adults on a national research-only online panel, cooperation rate 40.5%
estimates.definition: Respondent's answer to how many of the news stories on social media they believed to be entirely made up (1 = none of them; 5 = all of them); numerator = those answering at least 'some'
estimates.misinfo_def: In this study, we define “fake news” as “news stories that are completely made up.”
estimates.source_quote: (44%) of the respondents believed that at least “some” of the stories on social media were fake, and 12% thought that “most” of the news on social media was made up.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Perceived amount of fake news on social media, self-reported on a 5-point 'none of them ... all of them' scale
estimates.moderator_quote: They were also asked how many of the news stories on social media or on online media they believed to be entirely made up (1 = none of them; 5 = all of them).
estimates.notes: Perceived-amount item, platform-split counterpart of the online-news row; same 'at least some' vs 'most' ambiguity. The stricter 'most' figure (12%) is not extracted as a separate row. The sentence opens 'News on social media was perceived to be even more saturated by fake news: nearly half (44%)...'; a running page header falls between 'nearly half' and '(44%)' in the extracted text, so the quote starts at the value.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Not extracted: perceived THREAT of fake news to Chinese society - 'a great deal' 27.7% and 'a fair amount' 44.4% (about 7 in 10) - a threat judgement, not an exposure or amount measure. (2) Not extracted: third-person / first-person perception figures (62.8% think fake news has a great deal or fair amount of influence on themselves, 33.3% on others; means 2.73 vs 2.14) - perceived influence, excluded like belief. (3) Not extracted: information overload item shares (60.8% cannot keep up, 57.6% no time to check accuracy, 54.6% trouble choosing, 47% hard to concentrate) - overload, not misinformation exposure. (4) Not extracted: support for regulation (81.3% / 88% / 90.9%) - policy attitudes. (5) Not extracted: figures the paper cites from OTHER studies (Allcott and Gentzkow's 15%; Chen 2006's 58% and 48.9%; Fu 2012's 39%) - R8 forbids values a paper cites from elsewhere. (6) The stricter perceived-amount categories ('most' of online news fake 10%; 'most' of social media news fake 12%) are verbatim and could be added as stricter definition_variant rows if the adjudicator wants them. (7) No content, log or platform data anywhere in this paper: everything is self-report.

rob.design: National online survey, 2-6 August 2018, 1,111 Chinese adults from 22 provinces, 5 autonomous regions and 4 municipalities, recruited from a research-only online panel run by Impression Boguan Network Technology (Beijing) / Sina Data Solution, incentivised with an Alipay voucher; cooperation rate 40.5%. Sample 50.3% women, median age 40-49, 63% with at least some college, median monthly income CNY 6,000-8,000; the authors say it compares favourably with CNNIC's contemporaneous survey of Chinese internet users but skews more female, younger, better educated and higher income, and caution against generalising to the whole population. All misinformation measures are single self-report items on 4- or 5-point scales; no coder reliability applies. Scale reliabilities reported for the derived indices (information overload alpha .79, composite reliability .81; regulation support alpha .59, composite reliability .70). Authors also flag the narrow 'completely made up' definition of fake news as a limitation.
rob.item6_quote: Fake news exposure: In this study, we define “fake news” as “news stories that are completely made up.” To measure encounters with and perceptions of fake news, respondents were asked how often they came across news stories that they thought were fake in the past 6 months and how often they had shared a news story on social media that later they found to be fake (1 = never; 4 = often).
rob.item10_quote: Nearly half (46.2%) of the respondents reported frequently coming across fake news stories in the past 6 months. More than one-third also said that they had “often” (5.7%) or “sometimes” (30.9%) shared news stories on social media that they later found to be fake.
